terms.meaning: one tab of an Excel file
a raw block of bytes, here the contents of an Excel file

sections.name: File setup, Row
sections.title: File imports and row shape
sections.what: Brings in the Excel library and defines a row as a record with text keys.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps the export's data shape loose so any tab can be written.

sections.name: cell
sections.title: Making a value cell-safe
sections.what: Turns a value into something Excel can store. Text, numbers and true or false stay as they are, empty becomes blank, and anything else such as a list or nested object becomes JSON text.
sections.why: Stated in the workbook export comment: nested evidence is serialised, never summarised.
sections.watch_out: Nested data becomes hard-to-read JSON in the sheet, so a reader must parse it by eye.

sections.name: sheetName
sections.title: Making valid sheet names
sections.what: Creates a sheet name Excel accepts: removes forbidden characters, cuts it to 31 characters, and adds a number if another sheet already has the name.
sections.why: Stated in the comment: Excel has these name rules.
sections.watch_out: Long tab names are cut, so distinct names can look alike in the sheet list.

sections.name: addTable
sections.title: Writing one tab as a sheet
sections.what: Creates one sheet with a column for every key found in any row, writes each row, bolds the header and freezes it. If there are no rows, it writes a note saying so.
sections.why: Likely reason: a shared column set keeps rows with different fields lined up.
sections.watch_out: A row missing a key gets a blank cell, and a misspelled key creates an extra column that looks like a real field.

sections.name: workbookXlsx
sections.title: Building the whole Excel file
sections.what: Builds the About sheet with the notice, version and translation rules, adds a sheet for each tab, adds the optional extra tables, and returns the file as bytes. A null workbook falls back to a notice saying none was recorded.
sections.why: Stated in the comment: one sheet per tab, plus calculations and reason signals.
sections.watch_out: Any top-level value that is not a list, notice or version becomes a two-column measure sheet, so new top-level values appear as extra sheets.

summary: Turns the research workbook, and optional calculation and reason tables, into an Excel file with one sheet per tab, a bold header row, and an About sheet.
purpose: Lets the owner open the research in Excel with values exactly as recorded.
why: Stated in the comment: values are written as recorded, and nested evidence is kept as JSON rather than summarised.
how: First, create the file with an About sheet holding the notice, version and translation rules. Second, write each tab as a sheet: a list becomes rows, the Segments tab is flattened with a segment column, and a plain object becomes a measure and value table. Third, add the optional Yard evidence, calculation and reason tables. Fourth, return the file as raw bytes.
inputs: The workbook object, which may be null, optional Yard evidence rows, calculation rows, reason rows, and a notice text.
outputs: A Buffer, meaning the raw bytes of an Excel file.
risks: Nested data becomes hard-to-read JSON text in cells. Sheet names longer than 31 characters are cut, so distinct tab names can look alike. Rows with different keys produce a union of columns, so a misspelled key creates an extra column.
debug: If a tab is missing, check its name for forbidden characters or a clash with another sheet name. If a cell shows bracketed text, it is nested data written as JSON. The export is covered by a test that reads the file back.
